E. AB 604 Is Unconstitutional Because the Legislature Failed 
to Adhere to the Constitutionally Mandated Waiting 
Period for New Legislation 
i. The Legislature’s Failure to Wait 30 Days Before 
Acting Upon AB 604 Does Not Conform to Our 
Constitution’s Defined Procedures 
Irrespective of whether AB 604 violates other constitutional 
mandates, the Legislature’s passage of AB 604 only 4 days after its contents 
were first introduced renders AB 604 unconstitutional and, consequently, 
requires that ACA 8 be removed from the November ballot. 
California Constitution, Article IV, § 8(a) imposes an unambiguous 
requirement: 
At regular sessions no bill other than the budget bill may be 
heard or acted upon by committee or either house until the 31st 
day after the bill is introduced unless the house dispenses with 
DX234-0038
DCCC App. 298

29
this requirement by rollcall vote entered in the journal, three 
fourths of the membership concurring. 
Constitutional provisions are to be construed like statutes. (See Silicon 
Valley Taxpayers’ Ass’n, supra, 44 Cal.4th at p. 448; Bowens v. Superior Ct. 
(Alameda) (1991) 1 Cal.4th 36, 46; Lungren v. Deukmejian (1988) 45 Cal.3d 
727, 735 [citing Stanton v. Panish (1980) 28 Cal.3d 107, 115]; Bd. of 
Supervisors v. Lonergan (1980) 27 Cal.3d 855, 863; Amador Valley Joint 
Union High Sch. Dist. v. State Bd. of Equalization (1978) 22 Cal.3d 208, 
244–245.) Thus, when interpreting constitutional provisions, “[w]ellestablished rules require [this Court] to . . . ascertain the intent of the enacting 
legislative body so that [it] may adopt the construction that best effectuates 
the purpose of the law. ” (Hassan v. Mercy Am. River Hosp. (2003) 31 Cal.4th 
709, 715 [citing Esberg v. Union Oil Co. (2002) 28 Cal.4th 262, 268]; Klein 
v. United States (2010) 50 Cal.4th 68, 77 [citing Hassan]; Chavez v. City of 
Los Angeles (2010) 47 Cal.4th 970, 986 [same].) Although this Court must 
first begin with the text of a provision (Hassan, supra, 31 Cal.4th at p. 715), 
“[l]iteral construction [of the provision] should not prevail if it is contrary to 
the legislative intent apparent in the statute” (Lungren, supra, 45 Cal.3d at p. 
735), and this Court should avoid “judicial construction that renders part of 
[a provision] ‘meaningless or inoperative.’ ” (Hassan, supra, 31 Cal.4th at 
pp. 715–716 [quoting Mfrs. Life Ins. Co. v. Superior Ct. (San Francisco) 
(1995) 10 Cal.4th 257, 274].) 
The plain language of Article IV, § 8(a) mandates that neither house 
of the Legislature may hear or act upon a “bill” until the 31st day after its 
introduction. This waiting period serves two distinct purposes. 
First, the period exists to “giv[e] the interested public time to review 
the [legislative] proposal.” (Mission Hosp. Reg. Med. Ctr. v. Shewry (2008) 
168 Cal.App.4th 460, 492.) Were either house to introduce and act upon a 
measure on the same day or within just a few days, members of the public 
DX234-0039
DCCC App. 299

30
would be deprived of any meaningful time to review the measure’s contents, 
contact their representatives, and voice their approval or disagreement. That 
is why, in 1962, a proposal to shorten this period from 30 days to 20 days 
was rejected. Members of the public indicated that the full 30 days was 
required to provide them with sufficient time to “review legislation” and, in 
the case of public-facing organizations, notify their members “of the 
pendency of measures in which they are interested.” (Cal. Const. Rev. 
Comm’n, Constitution Revision History & Perspective 29 (1996) [available 
at: https://www.californiacityfinance.com/CCRChistory.pdf].) 
Second, the provision serves the practical purpose that legislators 
themselves must have adequate time to review a proposed measure before 
they are called upon to speak intelligently about its contents and implications, 
as well as vote on it. 
Thus, Article IV, § 8(a) affords the public and legislators sufficient 
time to evaluate proposed legislation, and any legislation passed without 
permitting such a period of public review is unconstitutional. 
Several of the Petitioners previously challenged the Legislature’s 
action on AB 604 on the grounds that the Legislature’s introduction and 
referral of the redistricting scheme on August 18, 2025, violated this 
provision. (Emergency Pet. for Writ of Mandate or Other Extraordinary or 
Immediate Relief to Stay Legislative Action with Respect to AB 604 and SB 
280, as Amended on August 18, 2025, S292490 (Cal. Aug. 18, 2025).) This 
Court denied that petition, concluding that those Petitioners had “failed to 
meet their burden of establishing a basis for relief at this time under 
California Constitution article IV, section 8.” (Disposition, S292490 (Cal. 
Aug. 29, 2025) [emphasis added].) 
For the purposes of this challenge, there are only two potential time 
periods to consider: the time period after legislation is introduced, when it is 
prematurely acted upon by the Legislature but has not yet been

and the time period after legislation has been introduced, prematurely acted 
upon, and signed—which is the time in which this Petition has been filed. 
Accordingly, this challenge must now be ripe for the Court’s consideration. 
The Legislature’s decision to refer the new legislation in AB 604 to 
committee and to debate it and pass it before the expiration of the 
Constitutionally required 30-day public review period constitutes a direct 
violation of the prohibition in Article IV, § 8(a). 
Although AB 604 was formally introduced on February 13, 2025 (see 
Exhibit 2), amending AB 604 on August 18, 2025, by removing all of its text
and replacing that language in toto with provisions that define a new 
constitutional map constitutes the introduction of new legislation subject to 
the 30-day rule in Article IV, § 8(a). California Courts have not addressed 
whether this tactic, known as “gut and amend,” satisfies Article IV, § 8(a).
Other states have been clear that the state legislature may not employ such a 
strategy to avoid constitutional obligations. (League of Women Voters of 
Honolulu v. Hawaii (Haw. 2021) 499 P.2d 382, 406; Washington v. Dep’t of 
Pub. Welfare (Pa. 2018) 188 A.3d 1135, 1151–1152; see Bevin v. Kentucky 
ex rel. Beshear (Ky. 2018) 563 S.W.3d 74, 92–94.) But more importantly, to 
condone this tactic would mean interpreting Article IV, § 8(a)’s 30-day 
waiting period as absurdly limiting the People’s right to know a mere bill 
number exists, rendering the 30-day requirement meaningless and 
insignificant. Such an interpretation thwarting the purpose of the provision 
is belied by the Constitution only allowing the Legislature to bypass the rule 
if fully three quarters of the Legislators vote to make an exception. Such an 
interpretation is squarely foreclosed by this Court’s precedent. (See Hassan, 
supra, 31 Cal.4th at pp. 715–716.) 
Another weak argument easily dispatched is that the Legislature need 
only comply with the 72-hour rule in Article IV, § 8(b)(2) of our State

32
Constitution. The 30-day rule focuses on the beginning of the legislative 
process and protects the public and legislators by permitting them a period 
of time to review the original draft of proposed legislation and consider their 
positions before it can be debated and amended. The 72-hour rule, by 
contrast, focuses on the end of the legislative process and requires that the 
final text of a bill be disclosed at least 72 hours before it is passed, ensuring 
legislators have time to see the text they will be voting upon. (Cal. Const. art. 
IV, § 8(b)(2) [“No bill may be passed or ultimately become a statute unless 
the bill with any amendments has been printed, distributed to the members, 
and published on the Internet, in its final form, for at least 72 hours before 
the vote . . . .” [emphasis added]].) There is no basis in the text of the 
Constitution, the canons of interpretation, the precedent of this Court, or 
logic to interpret the 72-hour rule as somehow superseding or making 
redundant the 30-day rule. They are prescribed in separate provisions and in 
every respect apply to different documents (original versus final proposed 
legislation) for different purposes. 
Article IV, § 8(a), appropriately construed, would have required the 
Legislature to wait until September 18, 2025, before taking any action with 
respect to AB 604. Because the Legislature passed AB 604 on August 21, 
2025, well before that date, AB 604 was enacted in conflict with Article IV, 
§ 8(a). As such, the act itself is unconstitutional. (See Hotel Emps. & 
Restaurant Emps. Int’l Union v. Davis (1999) 21 Cal.4th 585, 602 [“A statute 
inconsistent with the California Constitution is, of course, void.”]; People v. 
Navarro (1972) 7 Cal.3d 248, 260 [“Wherever statutes conflict with 
constitutional provisions, the latter must prevail.”].) 
ii. The Enrolled Bill Rule Should Not Preclude 
Judicial Review of AB 604 
Nearly a century ago, this Court articulated its view that “a statute, 
properly enrolled and authenticated, conclusively establishes, not only the 
DX234-0042
DCCC App. 302

33
contents of the law, but the due performance of all steps requisite to its 
passage by the Legislature.” (Taylor v. Cole (1927) 201 Cal. 327, 332.) But 
this principle is not absolute. Traditionally, the Enrolled Bill Rule may 
preclude judicial review of enrolled legislation, but it may only do so only 
“when an act of the Legislature is valid on its face . . . .” (People ex rel. Levin 
v. Cnty. of Santa Clara (1951) 37 Cal.2d 335, 337.) Thus, this Court has held 
that if it appears from the face of an enrolled bill that the act was adopted in 
violation of a constitutional mandate, this Court is permitted to invalidate the 
act on the basis of that violation. (See People ex rel. Conklin v. City of San 
Buenaventura (1931) 213 Cal. 637, 642, overruled on other grounds by 
Costa, supra, 37 Cal.4th at p. 1014, fn. 20 [Where it “appears on the face of 
[an] Assembly concurrent resolution . . . that one of the essential steps 
required by the Constitution . . . was not taken . . . we are compelled to hold 
that the [act], not having been legally adopted, its purported approval by the 
Legislature amounts to nothing.”]; Santa Clara Cnty. v. Superior Ct. (Santa 
Clara) (1949) 33 Cal.2d 552, 558 [approving of this Court’s holding in City 
of San Buenaventura that the constitutional sufficiency of a legislative act 
“may be tested by some appropriate proceeding”].) 
AB 604 was first introduced on February 13, 2025, and functioned to 
repeal an “obsolete” provision that required “county elections officials to 
update a voter’s registration record if change-of-address information 
indicates the voter has moved to a new residence address in California.” 
(Exhibit 2, at 1.) On August 18, 2025, the original text of AB 604 was deleted 
and replaced with the wholly different text and subject of AB 604 that is at 
issue here, regarding the boundaries of congressional districts through 2030 
(See generally Exhibit 3), and on August 21, 2025, the bill was passed by the 
Legislature. 
As discussed above, well-settled principles of constitutional 
construction establish that this practice violated Article IV, § 8(a) and 
DX234-0043
DCCC App. 303

34
deprived the people of California of their constitutional right to 30 days’ 
notice of new legislation. Those principles would require that this Court 
interpret § 8(a) as requiring that legislation be considered a newly introduced 
“bill” when a prior bill is wholly amended to address an entirely different 
subject, and deem the date of that legislation’s introduction to be the day of 
the “gut and amend” amendment. None of the requisite facts demonstrating
a violation of Article IV, § 8(a) are subject to dispute or inconsistent with the 
Legislature’s own official records. 
This Court’s application of the Enrolled Bill Rule under these 
circumstances to preclude review of the Legislature’s aggressive violation of 
Article IV, § 8(a) raises the question as to whether Article IV, § 8(a) is 
effectively a dead letter. No bill gutted and amended like AB 604 would ever 
be subject to review for compliance with Article IV, § 8(a). (This Court also 
concluded in an order issued on August 20, 2025, that a writ challenging AB 
604 for this same reason before enrollment was premature.) 
The Enrolled Bill Rule, holding that the enrollment of legislation 
creates presumption that legislative procedures were followed, is a judicial 
doctrine with English roots that predates the U.S. and California constitutions
that has been invoked to avoid litigation disputing whether a legislature 
followed its procedures to enact legislation, such as whether it published the 
correct statutory text or miscounted its votes. (United States v. 
Thomas (7th Cir. 1986) 788 F.2d 1250, 1253, cert. denied, (1986) 479 U.S. 
853 [citing Field v. Clark (1892) 143 U.S. 649 [“If a legislative document is 
authenticated in regular form by the appropriate officials, the court treats that 
document as properly adopted.”]]; United States v. Farmer (2d Cir. 2009)
583 F.3d 131, 151–152 [enrollment as a conclusive record of a statute]. The 
longstanding rule in California, as well as less than half the states, is that this 
presumption is conclusive. (See Taylor v. Legislature (1927) 201 Cal. 327, 
332; I C. Sands, Sutherland Statutory Construction § 15.03 et seq. (4th ed. 
DX234-0044
DCCC App. 304

35
1972); 82 C.J.S. Statutes § 83 (1953); 72 Am.Jur.2d Statutes § 90 (1974); 
and 4 A.L.R.2d 978 (1949)); Chris M. Micheli, Challenging the Enrolled Bill 
Rule: A Proposed Middle Ground for California, National Law Review (Jan. 
12, 2022) [available at: https://natlawreview.com/article/challengingenrolled-bill-rule-proposed-middle-ground-california].) However, other 
courts, including those in Pennsylvania and Kentucky, have held that the 
presumption is rebuttable. (See Consumer Party of Pa. v. Pennsylvania, 507 
A.2d 323 (Pa. 1986); D&W Auto Supply v. Dep’t of Revenue (Ky. 1980) 602 
S.W.2d 420.) 
There are sound grounds for distinguishing the application of the rule 
in this case from the general rule. While, under the separation of powers 
doctrine (Cal. Const. Art. III, § 3), this Court is rightly reluctant to interfere 
in matters of the Legislature’s compliance with its internal rules and 
compliance with mere procedure after a bill is enrolled, the Court also has 
the authority if not the duty to protect the rights of the people by enforcing 
rules in the Constitution that, like Article IV, § 8(a), limit the power of the 
Legislature to protect the people. That is, in a situation where the 
Constitution itself protects the people by imposing a limit on the 
Legislature’s power, as in the 30-day publication requirement in Article IV, 
§ 8(a), the Court is not unduly interfering in the Legislature’s internal affairs. 
Particularly where, as here, the Legislature’s violation of the state 
Constitution is evident from its own official published records, an alleged 
violation is justiciable without infringing upon the prerogatives of the 
Legislature. 
Accordingly, we urge this Court to expand the exception to the 
Enrolled Bill Rule for constitutional violations on the face of a bill to the 
circumstances presented here, where the Legislature’s own undisputed 
records—showing the wholesale gutting and amending of a prior bill to 
introduce significant new legislation just days before passage and enrollment

36
establish the Legislature’s clear violation of Article IV, § 8(a) in derogation 
of the people’s rights under the California Constitution to 30 days’ notice of 
new legislation.

Because the Legislature took action on a bill within 30 days of its 
introduction, AB 604 was enacted in violation of Article IV, § 8(a) and is 
invalid. The Court should therefore enjoin the Secretary from placing ACA 
8 on the ballot. 
III. CONCLUSION 
A ballot measure that would give effect to an unconstitutional statute 
is itself unconstitutional and may not be submitted to the voters. (See Weber, 
supra, 16 Cal.5th at p. 252.) Allowing ACA 8 onto the ballot would not only 
pose to the voters an illegal dual-subject question; it would condone an 
unlawful redistricting effort by the Legislature. The Legislature has engaged 
in a redistricting process before the voters have transferred redistricting 
power back to it and, while doing so, violated several fundamental 
constitutional restrictions on redistricting efforts. By engaging in this 
unlawful effort in the middle of the decade, the Legislature is also unlawfully
subjecting Californians to precisely the burden, tumult, and disruption that 
the Constitution was amended to prohibit more than once every ten years. 
For the reasons stated above, a writ of mandate requiring Respondent 
to refrain from taking any steps to place ACA 8 on the November 4, 2025, 
ballot should issue as prayed for, together with such other and further relief 
this Court deems just and proper.

We are pleased to submit this proposed congressional map to the California legislature for their 
consideration. We strongly believe that this map serves the best interest of California voters, 
while also attempting to push back against the corrupt scheme occurring in Texas and other 
Republican-majority states where Republicans – doing the bidding of their DC party bosses – 
are considering adopting a clearly racially gerrymandered, partisan map at the expense of their 
voters. 
Our proposed map was created using traditional redistricting criteria, consistent with guidelines 
laid out by the California’s Citizen Redistricting Commission. It allows for more compact 
districts than in the current Commission-drawn map, keeps more communities and 
neighborhoods together, splits fewer cities, and makes minimal disruptions to the Commissiondrawn map so as to impact as few residents as possible. This is a striking contrast from Texas’ 
proposed gerrymander which redrew all but one of their 38 congressional districts to minimize 
the state’s growing minority voting strength. 
Democrats cannot sit idly by while Texas Republicans and their DC party bosses attempt to 
steal congressional seats and rig the election in their favor, well before any votes have been 
cast. Unlike what Texas Republicans are attempting to do in letting politicians choose their own 
voters, we believe that voters should be able to decide who represents them.

OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
BACKGROUND
U.S. CONGRESS
U.S. Congress. The U.S. Congress is the part of the 
federal government that makes laws. Congress has 
two parts: the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of 
Representatives (House). Each of the 50 states is 
represented by 2 senators, with 100 senators in 
total. The House has 435 members. The number 
of representatives in the House for each state 
depends on how many people live in that state. 
Each member in the House represents an area of 
the state called a congressional district. California 
currently has 52 congressional districts. Voters 
who live in each congressional district elect one 
member of the House every two years to represent 
them. The next election for all 435 representatives 
will be in 2026. 
U.S. Census Counts States’ Populations Every Ten 
Years. The number of people living in an area goes 
up and down over time. Every ten years, the U.S. 
Census counts the number of people who live in 
the U.S. The last census was in 2020, and the next 
census is in 2030. This count is used to determine 
how many people live in each state and how many 
representatives in the House each state gets for the 
next ten years. 
CONGRESSIONAL REDISTRICTING
Each State Draws Congressional District Maps 
Following the U.S. Census. Every ten years, after 
the U.S. Census is completed, states draw new 
congressional district maps to reflect their number 
of House representatives and where people live. 
This process is called “redistricting.” Each state 
decides what process to use to draw its new 
district maps. When drawing new maps, each 
state must follow federal laws. For example, each 
congressional district in the state must represent 
about the same number of people. 
States Typically Do Not Redistrict Sooner Than 
Every Ten Years. States typically only draw 
congressional district maps every ten years, unless 
a court orders changes to comply with the law. 
In August 2025, however, the Texas Legislature 
passed a bill to adopt new maps for the 2026 
elections without a court order. Several other states 
also are considering changes to their maps before 
the 2026 elections. 
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
The text of this measure can be found on page 18 and the Secretary of State’s website at 
voterguide.sos.ca.gov.
• In response to Texas’ mid-decade partisan 
congressional redistricting, this measure 
temporarily requires new congressional 
district maps, as passed by the Legislature 
in August 2025, to be used in California’s 
congressional elections through 2030.
• Retains California’s independent Citizens 
Redistricting Commission and directs the 
Commission to resume enacting congressional 
district maps in 2031 after the 2030 census and 
every ten years thereafter.
• Establishes state policy supporting use of fair, 
independent, and nonpartisan redistricting 
commissions nationwide.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST’S ESTIMATE OF NET 
STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:

be to update election materials to reflect new 
congressional district maps.

ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST CONTINUED
Congressional Redistricting in California. State 
legislatures draw congressional district maps in 
most states, but some states use commissions to 
do this job. Before 2010, the California Legislature 
drew the state’s congressional district maps. 
In 2010, California voters gave this job to an 
independent commission known as the California 
Citizens Redistricting Commission (Commission). 
The Commission includes 14 members: 
5 Democratic members, 5 Republican members, 
and 4 members who are not registered with either 
of those political parties. When the Commission 
draws new congressional district maps, it must 
follow federal and state laws. For example, state 
law requires, among other things, the Commission 
to avoid splitting up neighborhoods or local 
communities of interest to the extent possible. 
State law also prohibits the Commission from 
considering political parties, current office holders, 
or people running for office when it draws the 
maps. 
Current California Congressional Districts. The 
Commission drew the current maps for California’s 
52 congressional districts. These maps were based 
on the 2020 U.S. Census and have been used since 
the 2022 congressional elections. 
PROPOSAL
CALIFORNIA’S CONGRESSIONAL DISTRICT MAPS
Use Legislatively Drawn Congressional District 
Maps Until After the Next Census. Proposition 50
replaces California’s current congressional district 
maps with new, legislatively drawn maps. (The total 
number of districts would not change.) Proposition 
50’s maps must follow federal law, but they are not 
required to follow the state requirements placed on 
the Commission. The state would use Proposition 
50’s maps for congressional elections starting in 
2026. The state would use these maps until the 
Commission draws new district maps, following the 
2030 U.S. Census. 
NATIONAL CONGRESSIONAL REDISTRICTING
Call for Change in Federal Law. Proposition 50
asks the U.S. Congress to change federal law and 
propose an amendment to the U.S. Constitution to 
require redistricting be done by “fair, independent, 
and nonpartisan redistricting commissions 
nationwide.” Proposition 50 expresses voter 
support for this idea, but does not change federal 
law or require any particular action of Congress or 
the California Legislature.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Minor One-Time Costs to County and State 
Elections Officials. Counties run elections, and the 
state oversees them. Because most congressional 
districts in California would change at least some 
under the new maps, county and state elections 
officials would need to update election materials. 
This would result in one-time costs to counties of 
up to a few million dollars statewide and one-time
costs to the state of roughly $200,000. The state 
amount is much less than one-tenth of 1 percent 
(0.1 percent) of the state’s roughly $220 billion 
General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the 
account the state uses to pay for most public 
services, including education, health care, and 
prisons.)

Tips for California’s Military and Overseas Voters
Taking part in elections is more convenient than ever for Californians serving in the military or living 
outside the United States. It begins when you register to vote as a military or overseas voter and receive 
election materials by mail, fax, or email. Be prepared!
• Start early. California’s county elections officials must send ballots to military and overseas 
voters no later than 45 days before Election Day. Fill out a voter registration application early at 
registertovote.ca.gov to ensure that you receive your voting materials in time and can return your 
voted ballot by Election Day.
• Know your options. When registering to vote as a military or overseas voter, you can choose to 
have your ballot mailed, faxed, or emailed to you. Additionally, you may visit your county elections 
official’s website for information about how to download your ballot and election materials. You may 
return your voted ballot to your county elections official by mail or, in certain circumstances, by fax. 
If you meet the requirements to return your ballot by fax, you must also fax the Oath of Voter form 
(available from your county elections official) waiving your right to a confidential ballot.
Alert! The Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP) has discontinued their service of 
faxing military and overseas voters’ election materials to county elections officials. 
What this means: you can no longer send your voted ballot to fax@fvap.gov. 
If you wish to return your voted ballot by fax, you must send it directly to your county 
elections official. 
• Stay in touch. Once you register as a military or overseas voter, you will continue to receive a ballot 
and election materials from your county elections official before each statewide election. However, 
you will need to update your voter registration if you change your address, your name, or your 
political party preference. Visit sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/military-overseas-voters/ for 
more election resources designed especially for you.
Dates to remember:
October 20, 2025: Last day for military and overseas voters to register to vote for the Statewide Special 
Election.

information.

Check Your Voter Status Online
Visit the Secretary of State’s My Voter Status page at 
voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to check your voter status, find your polling 
place or a vote center, and much more. 
To check your voter status, you will need to enter your first name, last name, date of birth, and 
your California driver’s license or California identification card number, or the last four digits of 
your social security number.
Visit voterstatus.sos.ca.gov for important voter details. 
What if I forgot to register to vote or update my registration?
No problem! If you missed the October 20, 2025, voter registration deadline, California 
law allows you to register to vote and vote until 8:00 p.m. on Election Day at your county 
elections office or at any voting location in your county. This process is called Conditional Voter 
Registration (CVR) and is commonly referred to as Same Day Voter Registration. 
Provisional Voting
Name not on the voter list at the polling place or the vote center?
You still have the right to vote with a provisional ballot.
What is a provisional ballot?
A provisional ballot is a regular ballot placed in a special envelope prior to being put in the 
ballot box. Provisional ballots are ballots cast by voters who believe they are registered to vote 
even though their names are not on the official voter registration list at the polling place or 
vote center.
A voter may need to cast a provisional ballot if they want to vote in person at a polling 
place or vote center but did not receive their vote-by-mail ballot or if they do not have their 
vote-by-mail ballot with them to surrender prior to voting in person.
Will my provisional ballot be counted?
Yes, your provisional ballot will be counted after elections officials have confirmed that you are 
registered to vote in that county, and you did not already vote in that election.
A provisional ballot may be used at any polling place or vote center in the county in which you 
are registered to vote. Only the election contests you are eligible to vote for will be counted.
How can you check the status of your provisional ballot?
Anyone who casts a provisional ballot has the right to find out from their county elections 
official if the ballot was counted and, if not, the reason why it was not counted.
You can check the status of your provisional ballot at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov.

CA MID-DECADE REDISTRICTING
The effort undertaken do adjust the Congressional District Boundaries 
adopted by the California Citizens Redistricting Commission keeps fidelity with 
the 2021 Process
• US Constitutional / Federal Law – Equal Population / VRA
• Contiguity – literal and functional criteria
• Communities of Interest - Must preserve identified communities of 
interest when possible.
• Cities and Counties - Respect city and county boundaries
• Compactness - Districts should not bypass nearby populations to grab 
distant ones.

CA MID-DECADE REDISTRICTING
Adjustments to the California Congressional Districts are built from multiple 
sources.
• Actual 2021 CRC Commissioner testimony on draft maps or 
instructions for mapping options given to staff
• Public maps presented to the commission
• Public testimony to the commission
• Draft or completed 2021 or 2011 Commission maps.

STRONG METRICS
This map is a reflection of state and federal requirements and California 
values. This is not a twitter map or an over-reach.
• This plan currently splits only 57 cities, which is fewer than the commission 
drawn plan.
• Using Polsby Popper as a metric for compactness, the minimum and 
maximum values are better in the public submission than the current 
commission plan. In other metrics, including Reock, Schwarzberg and 
Alternate Schwarzberg, the plan’s least-compact districts are more compact 
than the commission plan. 
Exhibit 523 - 4

These maps are an ADJUSTMENT of the existing Citizens Redistricting 
Commission drawn maps. 
• 8 districts are not touched at all, another 20 have less than 10% change.
• No changes were made to the map that were not consistent with the goals 
set forward by the delegation – pushing back on the mid-decade 
redistricting plans from Texas and other states.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
In June of this year, President Donald Trump called Texas Governor Greg Abbott and told 
him he wanted five more Republican districts. This started a mid-decade redistricting arms 
race that has the potential to give Republicans enough new seats to decide control of 
Congress after the 2026 election.
A month later, Governor Gavin Newsom told Jon Favreau and Tommy Vietor of Pod Save 
America that while he supported independent redistricting, he also knew he needed to fight 
back – to fight fire with fire. This started a movement in California that has led to today’s 
submission of a potential redistricting map to the State of California Assembly Speaker and 
Senate Pro Tempore, for their consideration.
The attached public submission meets Texas seat-for-seat. If they are going to perform a 
mid-decade redistricting to put five Democratically held seats into the Republican column, 
we can target five Republican seats in return.
At the same time, we have the ability to do something that Texas does not – we can create 
partisan improvements for current Democratic oOiceholders, protecting these seats for 
2026 and future elections.
Texas has already done a partisan gerrymander in 2021 when their plan received an “F” 
grade for fairness from the nonpartisan Gerrymandering Project. So, they have already 
pushed for partisan gain, and they are now attempting to squeeze out more Republican 
seats. At some point, this strategy will fail as they weaken their current Republican oOice 
holders in order to flip Democratic seats.
The last time California did a partisan redistricting was in 1991. As a result, using a 
partisanship criteria, we have many more opportunities to bolster the Democratic share of 
the vote in current Democratically held seats in addition to flipping Republican-held seats. 
As this plan will show, California can match or improve over Texas and can do it following 
the highest standards in redistricting criteria.
While this map is a response to Texas and other states that are doing some of the most 
egregious gerrymandering in the country, this map is reflective of how California does 
redistricting – with values – protecting the Voting Rights Act, preserving county, city and 
neighborhood boundaries, protecting communities of interest, and creating shapes that 
are compact.

This plan splits fewer cities than Texas’ plan, and even fewer cities than the Citizen’s 
Redistricting Commission (CRC) plan it replaces. It also is more compact than either the 
Texas plan or the 2021 CRC Plan.

The Criteria Used
From the beginning of this process, all involved in were committed to the values of 
Californians expressed through their legislature when they passed the state’s FAIRMAPS
Act for municipalities, voters when they implemented the Citizens Redistricting 
Commission (CRC) in 2008, and an even stronger vote for extending these responsibilities 
to congress in 2010. 
The required criteria includes the following:
• Equal Population
• Federal Voting Rights Act.
Exhibit 526 - 2
DCCC App. 460

• Contiguity 
• Preserving Communities of Interest 
• Geographic Integrity, reducing city and county splits 
• Compactness 
For equal population we stayed with the traditional one-person deviation common in 
congressional redistricting. This was based on the whole person count of the 2020 US 
Census as adjusted by the state for prison population.
The Voting Rights Act was utilized in a manner consistent with Citizen’s Redistricting 
Commission, with experts involved from the beginning of the process.
Contiguity was central to the creation of these districts, and we considered both the 
actual contiguity – areas that were touching, and functional contiguity, as, for example, 
where the Commission sought to draw Catalina Island with CA42 because it includes the 
points of departure for ferries that take residents and visitors to the island.
In state law a Community of Interest is defined as “a contiguous population which shares 
common social and economic interests that should be included within a single district for 
purposes of its eOective and fair representation.” 
We focus on communities of interest in all our local municipal redistricting, and we have 
conducted this work in nearly every county of the state, and in every region. And, as such, 
we bring to our short process a long history of working at the local level and hearing the 
concerns of residents as they approach the redistricting process.
In the CRC’s final report they state: 
“Public input is critical to respecting the geographic integrity of 
communities of interest, so the Commission launched the innovative 
public engagement tool, described above, that allowed Californians to 
tell the Commission about their communities, draw them on a map, 
and submit their comments directly to the Commission.” 
This means that the commissioners had access to information that was provided by an 
online portal to help guide their line drawing. This online portal is still available and was a 
valuable resource in our line drawing.
Throughout this process, we utilized actual commission testimony, public submissions, 
and resources from the CRC website at https://wedrawthelines.ca.gov/data-dashboard. In 
addition, we had members of the team who had spent hundreds of hours watching 
commission meetings over the past two redistricting cycles – giving them an expertise in

the communities throughout the state who have been involved in the process. The 
document that follows this summary outlines the communities of interest within each 
district that we changed and quotes actual 2021 public testimony that supports the 
changes we made.
The commission’s Geographic Integrity criteria is important, and it is an easily understood 
metric. The law states that:
“The geographic integrity of any city, county, city and county, local neighborhood, or 
local community of interest shall be respected in a manner that minimizes their 
division to the extent possible without violating the requirements of any of the 
preceding subdivisions.”
Our plan has 59 split cities, two fewer than the CRC in 2021. Some of these splits are zeropopulation but caused by so-called “islands” where a city may have a non-contiguous 
portion that is sometime miles away from the city core itself. There were some areas where 
we could fix a city split but didn’t because we were not making any changes in that district, 
and to make one small adjustment could be an undue burden for a local registrar who is 
otherwise not having any changes in their county.
Within cities, we sought to preserve neighborhoods. So, splits in San Jose, Sacramento, Los 
Angeles – all cities that were split by the commission, we followed neighborhood 
boundaries and/or city council district lines to ensure as much geographic integrity and 
protection of communities of interest in the map.
For compactness we considered the criteria utilized by the redistricting commission: 
“districts shall be drawn to encourage geographical compactness such 
that nearby areas of population are not bypassed for more distant 
population.” 
This is the lowest ranked commission criteria, and so, appropriately, it was not a priority 
focus in our eOorts. If there was a justification in any of the other criteria for a noncompact shape, we allowed ourselves to consider it, but when all choices were even, we 
would seek to adopt the most compact option.
While the state requirement is to have compactness based on a qualitative criterion, many 
who engage in redistricting may evaluate these maps based on quantitative metrics which 
are predominantly used around the country. And on these metrics the public submission 
performs well,

In addition to these criteria, we used partisanship to achieve the stated goals of this 
redistricting. In measuring partisanship we utilized three main datasets, the election 
results from the recent 2024 Presidential General Election, the 2022 Gubernatorial 
General, and Party registration in public voter files. These data points allowed us to 
determine the potential eOectiveness of new seats as we considered diOerent options.
Oftentimes, the process was to use the partisanship criteria as a rationale for a single shift 
of lines, but then in all the subsequent shifts we would utilize the traditional criteria. And 
we also refused to make some versions of districts that could improve partisan 
performance if to do so caused a major encroachment of the traditional criteria.
Respect for the 2021 Lines
The CRC is the gold standard for redistricting nationally. Over two successive decades the 
commission has utilized months of hearings, tens of thousands of public comments, and a 
fully transparent process to develop plans that were extremely eOective in reflecting the 
population of the state. Maps passed by the commission have been successful in fending 
oO multiple legal challenges and the 2021 plan was passed on a unanimous vote by five 
Democrats, five Republicans and four non-partisan commissioners.
In trying to combat the mid-decade redistricting in Republican states, including Texas and 
others, we sought to adjust the lines created by the CRC. This was not a complete redraw 
of the state. We retained the general structure of the plan passed by the commission in 
2021, leaving most districts completely untouched or adjusted less than 10%.
Throughout the process we utilized commission testimony, community of interest 
submissions and draft maps created by the commission to justify changes. As will be seen 
in the following district-by-district summary, for all districts we changed, we identified 
public comments which support the changes.
Measuring Democratic Performance
We utilized multiple measures to determine Democratic performance in these districts. 
The three main factors we looked at were partisan registration, the most recent presidential 
election between Donald Trump (R) and Kamala Harris (D), the 2022 gubernatorial contest 
between Gavin Newsom (D) and Brian Dahle (R) and voter registration files that identified 
partisanship.
Exhibit 526 - 5
DCCC App. 463

Using these metrics we determined that the commission plan had eight solid Republican 
seats with current Republican oOice holders, one Republican-leaning seat with a current 
Democratic oOice holder, five lean-Democratic seats with four Democrats and one 
Republican oOiceholder, and 39 solid Democratic seats. In the public submission map we 
find four solid Republican seats, two lean-Democratic seats, and 46 safe Democratic 
seats. The plan significantly increases opportunities for Democratic candidates going into 
the 2026 mid-term elections.
